title: If-sentences (Conditionals)
summary: The four types of if-sentences, which tenses go in each half, where the comma goes, the mistakes to avoid and how if-sentences make your writing more persuasive.

blocks.text: An **if-sentence** (also called a **conditional**) has two parts: the **condition** (the if part) and the **result** (what happens because of it). Each type uses a special pair of tenses.

rows: I would fly over the Red Sea.
If you heat ice, it melts.
If + present simple, will + base form
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If + past simple, would + base form
If I had wings, I would fly to the moon.
If + had + past participle, would have + past participle
If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.

blocks.title: How to choose the type
items: Can it **really** happen in the future? → **First**.
Is it **imaginary** or very unlikely now? → **Second**.
Is it about the **past**, which we cannot change? → **Third**.

blocks.text: When the **if-clause comes first**, put a **comma** after it. When it comes **second**, you do not need a comma.

items: If the bell rings, stop writing. (comma)
Stop writing if the bell rings. (no comma)

rows: You will miss the bus **unless** you hurry. (= if you do not hurry)
You can borrow my bike **as long as** you bring it back.
If only I had listened to my brother!
If I **were** you, I would apologise.

blocks.title: Watch out for these
items: If it will rain, we will stay home ✗ → If it rains, we will stay home ✓ (no will after if)
If I would be rich... ✗ → If I were rich... ✓
If I had a million pounds, I will buy a boat ✗ → ...I **would** buy a boat ✓ (second conditional: past + would)
If I would have known, I would have helped ✗ → If I **had known**, I would have helped ✓
Unless you don't hurry, you'll be late ✗ → Unless you hurry, you'll be late ✓ (unless already means if not)

blocks.text: If-sentences are not usually asked about directly in the reading questions, but you must **use them correctly in your writing**, where they show a range of sentence structures and verb forms (Grammar and punctuation).

blocks.title: If a reading question does mention one
items: Why does the writer begin this sentence with “If”? → to show what will happen as a result, often to warn or persuade the reader.
What does “If only I had stayed at home” tell you about the character? → they regret what they did.

rows: If we do nothing, our beaches will disappear.
If the water boils, turn down the heat.
If the centre were built here, traffic would increase.
I would be grateful if you could reply soon.

blocks.title: نصيحة سريعة
items: ممنوع will بعد if. قول If it rains مش If it will rain.
لو الجملة خيالية (لو أنا عندي جناحات...) استخدم If + ماضي ثم would.
لو بدأت الجملة بـ If، حط comma بعد الجزء الأول.

items.q: Correct: If it will snow, we will build a snowman.
items.a: If it **snows**, we will build a snowman.

items.q: Which type? If you mix red and yellow, you get orange.
items.a: **Zero conditional**: a fact that is always true (present + present).

items.q: Complete (first conditional): If you ______ (practise) every day, you ______ (improve).
items.a: If you **practise** every day, you **will improve**.

items.q: Complete (second conditional): If I ______ (be) the head teacher, I ______ (give) everyone a longer break.
items.a: If I **were** the head teacher, I **would give** everyone a longer break.

items.q: Complete (third conditional): If she ______ (check) her work, she ______ (not / make) that mistake.
items.a: If she **had checked** her work, she **would not have made** that mistake.

items.q: Add the missing comma: If you need help ask the librarian.
items.a: If you need help**,** ask the librarian.

items.q: Rewrite with unless: If you don't wear a coat, you will be cold.
items.a: Unless you wear a coat, you will be cold.

items.q: Write one if-sentence for a persuasive letter asking the council to plant more trees.
items.a: Example: If more trees are planted, our streets will be cooler and the air will be cleaner. (any correct first conditional is fine)
